title: The flower
hook: why it's fresh; impermanence on a plate

segments.voice: Yesterday, deepa, the lamp. Your line was one flame. Did you let one small light be the first one last night? Day one hundred and thirteen.

Walk past a Hindu temple early in the morning, in India or in New Jersey, and you'll often see the same thing near the gate. Someone selling flowers. Marigolds strung into long orange ropes. Jasmine in little bundles. A pile of red hibiscus. They'll all be gone by noon, and by tomorrow they'll be wilted. So why does anyone buy them? Why not a silk flower that lasts a year, dusted once a month? That's the question hiding on the third object of the shelf. Today: the flower.
screen: `FLOWER SELLERS AT THE GATE.` → `GONE BY TOMORROW.` → `WHY NOT A SILK ONE?`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is pushpa, flower. It's one of the most common offerings in puja, and it comes with a small set of habits that tell you what it's for. Many families pick or buy flowers fresh for the morning. Yesterday's flowers are taken down and replaced. A flower that fell on the ground is usually not offered. And many people don't smell a flower meant for the shrine: the first enjoyment of it isn't theirs. Different forms of the divine have their favorites. Red hibiscus is loved for Ganesha and for the Goddess. The lotus goes with Lakshmi. For Shiva, many offer the three-part leaf of the bilva tree. For Vishnu and Krishna, a leaf of tulsi, holy basil. And the offering doesn't have to be grand. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that when someone offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. Four of the simplest things on earth. The heart doing the offering is what's weighed. Now the part the flower teaches by itself. You set it down in the morning, and by evening it's drooping. You're offering something that won't last. That's not a flaw. It's honest. Everything on the plate, including the person holding the plate, is on its way somewhere. So you don't offer it once and keep it forever. You do it again tomorrow. Fresh, daily.
screen: `PUSHPA — THE FLOWER.` · `FRESH, NOT SMELLED FIRST.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WILTED BY EVENING, SO AGAIN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: If there's a flower or a leaf near you, a houseplant, a weed outside, a blossom on the table, take one gently, or just go and look at it where it grows. If not, picture one. Look at it closely. The color. The veins. The tiny imperfect edge. It won't look like this tomorrow. Now set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, next to a photo of someone you love. If you pray, you can offer it with a name you honor. Then just sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Pushpa. The flower: offered fresh, left unsmelled, gone by evening, and brought again the next day. Today's word.
Your line: fresh, daily. Today, pick one small thing you usually do on autopilot and do it fresh, as if for the first time. Day one hundred and thirteen.

howItsDone: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning, taking down the previous day's, and often choose flowers or leaves associated with a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, lotus for Lakshmi, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

original.note: Sanskrit puṣpa: flower. One of the classic offerings of puja.

trapdoor: what you thought: decoration for the shrine.
what it means: something fresh, offered before you enjoy it, that wilts by evening, so it's offered again tomorrow.
what a scholar hears: pushpa is one of the standard upacharas, the services of puja, and Gita 9.26 names leaf, flower, fruit and water as offerings accepted when given with devotion.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion)

notes: Customs described as 'many families' (fresh daily, not smelling flowers for the shrine, not offering fallen flowers) vary by family and region; confirm.
Deity-flower associations (hibiscus for Ganesha and the Goddess, lotus for Lakshmi, bilva for Shiva, tulsi for Vishnu/Krishna) are common but not universal; confirm.
'In India or in New Jersey' is a scene-setting line; adjust if a Keeper prefers another place.
